title: Bird Flu Is Raging on a Mink Farm. It Could Spark a Human Pandemic, Experts Say, but Officials Won’t Act.
author: Julie Leopo
content:
The strain of bird flu that's ripped through American barns for the last four
years has killed two people who caught it from sick animals. But as far as
anyone can tell, humans can't spread it. The virus has remained a true "bird"
flu, tailored to attach to avian cells, not invade human throats and noses,
where coughing and sneezing reliably spew droplets.

Under the right conditions, however, that could change. A [single
mutation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12633761/) could give the
bird flu a foothold in people and spark a pandemic that [experts
fear](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/25/opinion/bird-flu-america-death.html)
could be deadlier than COVID-19.

For that to happen, this bird flu would likely need to find an intermediate
host — an animal vulnerable to viruses that infect both birds and humans.
These animals would be crowded together, each infection raising the odds that
a new strain could arise through mutation. Then, for that strain to jump
across species, it would have to have access to humans and time to spread
among them undetected.  

That perfect petri dish exists right now, a ProPublica investigation found.
For over two months, an outbreak of bird flu has raged uncontrolled on a Utah
farm that raises thousands of mink for fur. Mink have lungs and airways that
on a cellular level are remarkably similar to those of people; they have
caught and spread other flus and infected some humans with COVID-19.

Instead of trying to stop the outbreak and prevent it from spilling into
humans, state and federal officials have done little except try to keep its
existence quiet, our investigation shows. The failure to act amounts to a
cascade of missteps flu experts called “irresponsible” and “puzzling.” One
called it “playing with fire.”

![A row of long, white-roofed agricultural buildings sits at the base of a
large, barren brown hill under a cloudy sky, viewed across a dry, grassy
field.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MINK-
LEOPO-2_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)C&T
Fenn Farms, a mink fur farm west of Provo, Utah, on Sept. 25 Julie Leopo for
ProPublica

Utah agriculture officials learned in mid-August that mink were dying of bird
flu on C&T Fenn Farms, about an hour’s drive south from Salt Lake City,
according to communications released under the state’s public records law.

Had poultry been infected, the playbook would have been clear: The strain is
so virulent that if a single chicken tests positive, the U.S. government
requires farmers to kill the whole flock to protect other farms as well as
public health. Poultry farmers are reimbursed for the loss.

But there are no federal rules for how to deal with sick mink.

Handling Utah’s response was state veterinarian Amanda Price, who sought help
from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which takes the lead on bird flu
outbreaks involving poultry and cows.

USDA officials said they didn’t regulate mink or have a vaccine that was
approved to give them. And though officials with the Centers for Disease
Control and Prevention spoke with Price’s health department counterparts who
were less involved with the outbreak, they never talked to her, and she never
reached out.

The threat of spillover has been far from the minds of Utah officials, records
and interviews show. Instead, front and center have been the interests of a
business raising animals to skin for luxury pelts to ship overseas.

"It has been devastating," Price told ProPublica of the outbreak and its
impact on the farm’s owner. "This is his life's work that he's seeing be
destroyed. I really hope that you understand the humanity behind this
situation."

Flu experts were unequivocal that the government should have ordered the farm
to cull its mink, [as other
countries](https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/finland-orders-
cull-50000-mink-foxes-due-bird-flu-2023-08-01/) [have
done](https://www.science.org/content/article/incredibly-concerning-bird-flu-
outbreak-spanish-mink-farm-triggers-pandemic-fears).

But Utah never seriously considered it. A fur trade representative warned
Price that doing so would kill the business and, ultimately, the industry.
Farms spend decades breeding mink to develop unique genetic lineages.

"There's just not a lot of options out there other than kind of sitting and
waiting and seeing what happens,” Price said, noting that USDA officials did
not urge her to kill the mink or make her feel like bird flu in mink was any
riskier than infections in other animals that have caught it, like ducks and
cows.

Flu experts found that response surprising.

“Every other country that I'm aware of that has had H5N1 in fur farms,
depopulation has happened pretty quickly,” said Tom Peacock, an avian
influenza researcher at the Pirbright Institute. "The fact that the first
instinct wasn't just to depopulate and figure stuff out later is very
concerning to me.”

And all the while, officials didn't monitor the mink workers for symptoms, as
guidance [from the CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/bird-
flu/php/surveillance/index.html) urges.

Their exposure is significant: Mink sneeze. They escape. They attack. “The
mink are fierce,” said a Spanish-speaking “minkero” who works on a nearby
farm, showing the scars he got from the aggressive, solitary creatures. “You
get scared because the fucking thing bites, and it claws at you.”

![A close-up view of a person’s bent arm, showing healed scars on the forearm
against a bright blue sky with scattered white
clouds.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MINK-
LEOPO-61_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=527)A
mink farmworker, sometimes referred to as a “minkero” among the Spanish-
speaking community, shows scars from mink bites and scratches in Payson, Utah.
Workers typically wear long gloves to protect themselves but can still be
bitten or scratched. Julie Leopo for ProPublica

Right now in Washington state, [officials are working to track down the
contacts](https://www.yakimacounty.us/DocumentCenter/View/46716/101526_Yakima-
County-Resident-Tests-Positive-for-Avian-Influenza) of a symptomatic person
exposed to dairy cattle infected with bird flu. The patient is isolating at
home. Utah public health officials used to do similar, proactive monitoring.
But they stopped after complaints from their colleagues in the agriculture
department that farmers were annoyed by it.

“Us doing active monitoring was making it so that farms didn’t want to work
with them,” said Pamela Gomez Pinedo, a respiratory disease epidemiologist for
Utah's health department. As a result, public health workers had a "pretty
difficult time" getting details from agriculture officials, she said.

As part of a [2025 agreement](https://epi.utah.gov/wp-content/uploads/Utah-
Zoonotic-Influenza-Interagency-Response-Plan_Apr-2025_signed.pdf), the Utah
Department of Agriculture and Food agreed to share information about bird flu
outbreaks on farms — so long as the health officials didn’t do anything to
track workers’ health.

"We will only do active monitoring in the case of evidence of human-to-human
transmission,” Pinedo said in emails with a CDC epidemiologist. As the
outbreak stretched to a month, CDC officials expressed concerns, asking how
anyone would know if a worker had been infected if they weren’t getting
tested.

Price said the state’s policy not to monitor workers is meant to allow farmers
to decide whether to contact the health department, rather than “forcing it on
them.” "If we started seeing people actively dying from this, obviously that
would change how we respond to this,” she said.

A telltale sign of bird flu infection in humans is eye redness. It is present
in over [90% of
cases](https://www.nejm.org/doi/10.1056/NEJMoa2414610?url_ver=Z39.88-2003&rfr_id=ori:rid:crossref.org&rfr_dat=cr_pub%20%200pubmed)
and is often the sole symptom a person displays.

Last Saturday, a ProPublica reporter tracked down two people who worked at the
Utah mink farm. One had a visibly red eye.

The CDC [explicitly urges testing for the symptom](https://www.cdc.gov/bird-
flu/php/surveillance/index.html).

After ProPublica reached out to the farm, its owner, Chad Fenn, contacted the
Utah County Health Department about the red eye, which had cleared up by
Monday, he told ProPublica. He said the worker got dust in his eye; the
department didn't recommend testing.

"They're not going to do anything,” Fenn said. “They said they don't see that
there's a need." He said the department recommended testing only if other
symptoms, like a cough or sore throat, developed.

A half dozen flu experts had no shortage of adjectives to describe their
disbelief at the government decisions not to cull the mink or monitor and test
the workers.

“It’s amazing to me,” said Gail Hansen, a former Kansas state public health
veterinarian and epidemiologist. “Utah doesn't want to be the epicenter of the
next human flu outbreak, right?”

* * *

Most of the new viruses that have shaken humanity in the past century have
spilled over from animals. Ebolas likely came from fruit bats; HIV, from
chimpanzees. The leading theory for COVID-19 is that it jumped from bats to
humans via an intermediate host mammal such as a raccoon dog. And all the
modern flu pandemics have been bird flu viruses that mutated to spread in
humans.

[ProPublica reported extensively on spillover in a 2023 series called “Roots
of an Outbreak.”](https://www.propublica.org/series/roots-of-an-outbreak) To
prevent more deadly spillovers, experts worldwide urge governments to take a
“[one health](https://www.who.int/health-topics/one-health#tab=tab_1)”
approach to viral threats, treating dangers to animals as dangers to humans.

That’s not happening in Utah, experts said after reviewing ProPublica’s
findings. Both the state and federal government are to blame.

"There's no leader of this 'one health' team to take charge," said Erin
Sorrell, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.
"That is going to allow the virus to continue to circulate, potentially adapt
and potentially spill over into another host, whether it's avian, mammalian or
human."

This strain of bird flu, which began ripping through American poultry farms in
early 2022, has proved adept at jumping to other species. It took hold in cows
in 2024 and since then has [run rampant through
dairies](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-
influenza/hpai-detections/hpai-confirmed-cases-livestock).

Yet [federal guidance](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/138754) to prevent the
spread into mink farms hasn’t considered cows a threat. Farmers are encouraged
to keep wild birds from infiltrating their barns and avoid feeding them raw
poultry. It has said nothing about feeding beef parts to mink, which farmers
commonly do in summer months to encourage the animals to put on weight and
grow.

Dairy cows, which are not “depopulated” if exposed to bird flu, [can still be
slaughtered](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/aphis-
requirements-hpai-livestock-2026.pdf) with the meat sold to farms and humans
even though [researchers have found the virus in the tissues of sick
cows](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/31/7/25-0134_article). USDA officials
have insisted that [beef for human consumption is free of bird
flu](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-
influenza/hpai-detections/livestock/testing-and-science/meat-safety), in part
because the virus concentrates itself in sections of the cow people don’t
usually eat. Fenn said that the mink are routinely fed raw organs of
livestock, including cows.

The [genomic
data](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/?term=A%2FMink%2FUT%2F26G11429)
from the samples of mink lungs and brains sent from Utah to a USDA lab shows
that the mink were stricken with the same strain of the virus that has spread
in dairy herds. Officials said they didn't know whether contaminated beef was
the way the mink got infected.

![Several cattle graze in a dry, grassy pasture with silhouetted trees and a
mountain ridge in the background.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/148A2659_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=1149)Cows
graze in a field in Utah Valley, Utah. Julie Leopo for ProPublica

In mink, the dairy strain of bird flu may have found a much better host for
mutating into a human flu, because mink airways have an abundance of the type
of cell receptors in people’s throats and noses that are a common pathway for
infection.  

[A 2024 study](https://www.scripps.edu/news-events/news/20241205-wilson-
paulson-h5n1/) of the dairy strain of the bird flu found that a single
mutation could switch the virus from preferring the bird-type receptors to
human-type receptors. And in [studies using
ferrets](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4810786/), a close relative
of mink, the virus acquired mutations that let it attack human-type cell
receptors.

It’s not clear to scientists just how much of an evolutionary leap would be
needed for this strain of bird flu to spread among humans, or whether mink are
the host that would allow that leap to happen.

How this ultimately plays out "really depends on what happens with the virus,"
said Meghan Davis, an epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins University.

"We might get lucky, and a response that is not robust may not have dire
consequences," she said. "But we may get unlucky."

There’s also a risk of something called “reassortment,” where another flu
virus could infect the same cell as a bird flu virus and swap wide swaths of
genetic code already adapted to humans.

When the outbreak in the mink farm started, there was very little seasonal flu
it could mix with, but September saw one of the [earliest starts to flu season
on record](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03150-8), compared with
November, when flu normally takes off.

"The most likely scenario for a pandemic is that we have a virus that
reassorts with another virus," said Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the Pandemic
Center at the Brown University School of Public Health. "Obviously, having
this circulate amid human flu season is not great."

Utah officials were far more responsive to the threat of spillover in 2020,
when outbreaks of COVID-19 spread explosively on mink farms – including this
very farm. They invited federal officials to the state to research how the
virus adapted and moved.

Given mink’s reputation as escape artists, wildlife experts set up traps
around infected farms. The traps frequently caught mink carrying COVID-19 that
had originated in the nearby barns. The virus infected [both escaped mink and
wild __ mink they had come in contact
with](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7920664/). Mink and farmworkers
were frequently tested, [tracking the way that the virus was spreading and
mutating](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9864593/).

[As other states](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10747742/) and
countries took the same measures, they identified [humans infected by the mink
with COVID-19](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-
news/item/2020-DON301) and, ultimately, human-to-human transmission.

There are no similar efforts now in Utah with bird flu.

A USDA spokesperson told ProPublica that it was more involved in 2020 because
the virus that causes COVID-19 had "significant" potential to transmit between
humans and animals and vice versa.

Scientists with the USDA sequenced and published bird flu genomic data from
the first samples of dead mink. Those sequences didn't show any particularly
concerning mutations, experts and the CDC told ProPublica.

But in the past two months, experts said, the virus is sure to have continued
mutating as it spread – it's only a question of whether those mutations could
confer some advantage in infecting humans as well.

"As long as it continues to go mink to mink, then it becomes more and more
likely that it could jump to a human," Hansen said.

Fenn said new samples were taken two weeks ago. Price said she is still
waiting for the results.

John Korslund, a retired USDA official who helped coordinate the response to
COVID-19 on mink farms several years prior, was one of several experts who
said officials need to look closely at newer genetic samples to see how the
virus is evolving.

"I really want to know what the virus has done, from when it started to
today,” he said. “Are we getting accumulated mutations making the virus more
dangerous?"

![A close-up view of an albino mink with white fur, reddish eyes and a pink
nose looking upward directly at the camera
indoors.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MINK-
LEOPO-43_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)Mink
have the type of cell receptors that a seasonal flu will target in human
throats and noses. Julie Leopo for ProPublica

* * *

ProPublica began reporting on the outbreak late this summer after the USDA
[updated a bird flu dashboard](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-
disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-detections/mammals?page=1) that showed
seven captive mink had tested positive in Utah. But neither the USDA nor state
officials had said anything publicly, and, when asked, they wouldn't discuss
what was actually happening on the farm.

Communications obtained under the state’s public records law — [first
published by the Animal Welfare Institute](https://awionline.org/news/records-
request-reveals-unhurried-inadequate-response-to-bird-flu-outbreak-in-utah-
farmed-mink/) and [reported on by the Salt Lake
Tribune](https://www.sltrib.com/news/2026/09/27/animal-advocates-raise-alarm-
over/) — show Utah officials took pains to protect the farm’s privacy amid the
outbreak. The state did [not declare an
emergency](https://ag.utah.gov/conservation/agricultural-loans/emergency-
disaster-relief-loan-program/), because doing so, officials said, "may alert
animal rights groups,” according to the messages.

Willy Lanier, a public health veterinarian with the state health department,
told colleagues to keep the outbreak under "closer hold" than outbreaks of
bird flu on poultry and dairy farms. Keeping the information confidential was
consistent with state protocol, a spokesperson in his department said, adding
that it was still shared with local health officials. But when ProPublica
reached out to the spokesperson for the Utah County Health Department about a
possible bird flu outbreak, she said, “That would be news to me.”

Price is so deferential to the family that owns the farm that she has not set
foot on the property.

> “We might get lucky, and a response that is not robust may not have dire
> consequences. But we may get unlucky.”
>
> Meghan Davis, Johns Hopkins University epidemiologist

“I’m really the only one here at this facility that's been dealing with the
producer. They're a very private bunch,” Price said. “A lot of what I'm going
off of is what I've seen from Google Maps, what I've talked to the producer
about, what I've talked to the vet about. I haven't felt the need to go out
there based on those conversations."

She said she "became very comfortable" in conversations with the owner that
the virus wouldn't spread off the farm. It doesn't have animals moving on and
off over the course of the year like on a dairy or poultry farm; mink leave
only when they're slaughtered and skinned for pelts at the end of the year.
She also said that she was confident the owner would recapture any escaped
mink.

Short of a formal quarantine, Price gave the farm a "verbal hold" to not move
any mink, or manure or carcasses, off the farm. "We haven't seen spread off of
this farm. We have not had additional cases in Utah that are linked to this,
so thus far the verbal hold orders and the measures that have been taken look
to be successful: There is not spread happening from this farm from this
case."

Price’s assertion didn't allay the concerns of experts that ProPublica spoke
with. When poultry test positive for this strain of bird flu, all nearby farms
are quarantined and tested for the virus. But the approach in Utah relies on
farms reporting cases or the public calling in reports of dead birds in the
area.

“If you’re not looking for something, you won't find it,” Sorrell said.
“Unless you’re doing active surveillance, you can’t claim that you haven’t had
cases.”

Fenn told ProPublica his conversations with state officials made him less
worried about any kind of spread. When the outbreak started, Fenn said, he
asked whether the bird flu could infect people.

"Right off the bat, the state people we reported to, they said you don't need
to worry too much,” Fenn said. "My guys wear masks every day. They have
glasses they can wear,” Fenn said. “ Me? I don't wear it at all. Never have,
never will, because I've been doing it for 40 years."

Fenn said he wished he could vaccinate the mink for bird flu to keep the rest
of his animals from catching it and dying; Price asked the USDA about a
vaccine that had been used to save [endangered wild
species](https://www.zoetis.com/news-and-insights/featured-stories/a-dose-of-
hope-for-hawaiian-monk-seals) but said she got nowhere with that request. The
USDA told ProPublica its division responsible for protecting animal health has
no “species-specific regulatory authority or dedicated programs” for
vaccinating mink, depopulating them or paying owners back for such a culling.

Fenn told ProPublica he thinks concerns about mink as a particularly risky
bird flu host are trumped up by anti-fur activists, the same forces that he
believed were behind the reactions in Spain and Finland, which depopulated
mink farms hit with bird flu. "Europeans are a little scared of everything,"
he said. "They're going to do what they're going to do, and here in the United
States, we're going to do what we're going to do."

Price said she was aware that Finland and Spain had depopulated their fur
farms when the same strain infected them. “I didn’t really look much further
into it,” she said, explaining that she was interested in those cases only for
lessons about how to handle the outbreak, but not the particular reasons those
countries chose to depopulate the farms.

A USDA spokesperson said Congress would have to specifically fund a program to
depopulate mink. (The program to cull poultry to stop the spread of bird flu
has cost well over $1 billion since 2022.)

The events in Utah are a "clear warning sign" about the dangers of mink farms,
said Neil Vora, executive director for the Preventing Pandemics at the Source
Coalition.

"Fur farms are to produce pelts purely for luxury goods, to make fancy coats,"
he said. "It's absurd that we're willing to gamble with the lives of millions
of people just to keep an industry alive."

The industry has struggled as American consumers increasingly reject fur.
Though domestic farms peaked about a decade ago, selling luxury pelts that
often ended up in China, foreign farms have sprung up, threatening the
business.

While [animal rights advocates have pushed](https://awionline.org/policy-
efforts/mink-virus-act/#/520/) for Congress to [adopt
legislation](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/2185)
that would phase out the fur industry, buying out farmers over the course of a
year to end the practice once and for all, winds in Congress are blowing the
other direction. The Senate will soon weigh in on the latest Farm Bill, which
now seeks to expand market opportunities for mink farmers [by undoing a
prohibition in federal law on subsidizing the fur
trade](https://spectrumnews1.com/wi/milwaukee/news/2026/05/11/farm-bill-mink-
farmers-wisconsin).

The virus continues to spread on the Utah farm, said Fenn, though at a slower
pace. Experts told ProPublica it still poses a risk.

"I would want a full on hazmat suit if I were on that farm,” Peacock said.
"Or, preferably, I'd rather not to be on that farm.”

Experts Say, but Officials Won’t
Act.](https://www.propublica.org/article/bird-flu-mink-farm-utah-human-risk)
